citation.title: A Physics-Informed Neural Network-based Topology Optimization (PINNTO) framework for structural optimization
citation.authors: Hyogu Jeong, Jinshuai Bai, Chanaka P. Batuwatta-Gamage, Charith Rathnayaka, Ying Zhou, YuanTong Gu
citation.arxiv_id: none found (arXiv API title and author searches, 2026-09-24)
citation.version_coded: Accepted author manuscript from QUT ePrints 237324 (eprints.qut.edu.au/237324/1/122042111.pdf, CC BY-NC-ND 4.0), 33 pages including the repository cover page, read in full; Figs. 7, 14 and 18 checked as page images. The version of record (ScienceDirect) was not read.

included.reason: I-QUALITY (screened I-UNCLEAR; the article claims design parity with SIMP and reports PINNTO as slower)

claim.primary_outcome_paraphrase: On four 40×20 compliance benchmarks, PINNTO designs reach compliance within 0.02-5.51% of 88-line SIMP designs (lower only in case 1), while each run takes 399-2,177 s against 0.3-1.6 s for SIMP.
claim.key_phrase: generate comparable designs to those produced by the current successful approaches
claim.location: Sec. 4.1, Fig. 7 and Table 1 (first quantitative comparison with a classical method; the Abstract claims comparable designs to SIMP without numbers, and Sec. 5 has no numbers); key phrase from the Abstract
claim.claimed_speedup_basis: Quality-stratum primary outcome, so no speed factor is entered (convention of all final non-speed records, e.g. adjudicated P00051 and P01813). Speed alternative, derived from Table 1, SIMP total time ÷ PINNTO total time: 0.81/915.02, 1.19/1,581.02, 1.56/2,176.68 and 0.31/398.86 give 0.00089, 0.00075, 0.00072 and 0.00078 (median 0.000765). PINNTO is about 1,130-1,395 times slower in total and about 1,200-1,700 times slower per iteration (32.01-36.26 s vs 0.02-0.03 s) [derived]. The authors state that PINNTO's computational time exceeds SIMP's.
claim.alternatives: (1) Table 1 as a speed outcome: PINNTO far slower than SIMP (see claimed_speedup_basis), which the authors acknowledge (Sec. 4.1). (2) Sec. 4.3, Fig. 14: compliance vs SIMP at meshes 10×10 to 120×120, PINNTO lower at 10×10 and similar elsewhere. (3) Sec. 4.6, Fig. 18: 3D cantilever (60×20×4), PINNTO 155.3196 vs SIMP 147.6219 (+5.2% relative to SIMP [derived]; the text says under 5%) in 45 vs 104 iterations, presented as faster convergence, with no times. (4) Abstract: optimized topologies without labelled data or FEA (qualitative).

baseline.classical_method: SIMP with sensitivity filter and optimality-criteria update, 88-line MATLAB code of Andreassen et al. [52] for the 2D validation; 3D SIMP code of Liu and Tovar [48] for the 3D case (Secs. 2.2, 4.1, 4.6)
baseline.implementation: 88-line MATLAB code (2D); Liu and Tovar 3D MATLAB code (3D); PINNTO in Python 3.9.5 with PyTorch 1.9.1+cpu (Sec. 3.2)
baseline.solver: SIMP: not stated. PINNTO: energy-based PINN (8 hidden layers × 80 neurons, Adam, 1000 epochs per TO iteration) replaces FEA (Sec. 3.2)
baseline.hardware_classical: Intel Core i7-10700 CPU @ 2.90 GHz, 16 GB RAM, stated for all numerical cases (Sec. 3.2)
baseline.hardware_ml: Same CPU (PyTorch CPU build), stated for all numerical cases (Sec. 3.2)
baseline.problem_size: 2D validation 40×20 elements (4 cases, volume fraction 0.5, 0.5, 0.5, 0.4); NN-size study 80×40; mesh study 10×10 to 120×120; passive elements 60×40; two loads 50×50; 3D cantilever 60×20×4 (Secs. 4.1-4.6)
baseline.classical_iterations: Convergence tolerance τ = 0.01% for the validation (Sec. 4.1; Sec. 3.1.2 states a 1% change criterion for PINNTO). SIMP 35, 49, 67, 11 iterations vs PINNTO 27, 46, 68, 11 (Table 1); 3D SIMP 104 vs PINNTO 45 (Fig. 18)
baseline.training_time: No offline training: the PINN is trained within every TO iteration (1000 epochs) and this cost is inside the Table 1 times [inferred from Secs. 3.1.2 and 3.2]
baseline.quality_metric: Mean compliance (objective value). For PINNTO it appears to be computed from the PINN displacement field, not by FEA of the returned design [inferred from Sec. 3.1.2 and the Sec. 4.3 discussion]; for SIMP by FEA.

R1.evidence: Sec. 4.1, Fig. 7, Table 1: both methods use the same 40×20 meshes, volume fractions, rmin = 3, p = 3, OC update and convergence tolerance; iteration counts and times are reported for both. Compliance is within 0.02-5.51%, PINNTO lower only in case 1. The parity claim is made at about 1,100-1,400 times the SIMP wall-clock [derived], so the unequal budget favours the ML side and is fully disclosed. [judgment: an adjudicator may prefer partial for the unequal budget]

R2.evidence: Stratum Q (PROTOCOL §11, 2026-09-24): R2 applies only through criterion (b). The abstract (AAM p. 1) names SIMP as the comparator and gives no numbers; the results use the same SIMP family (88-line code in 2D, Liu and Tovar code in 3D; Sec. 4.1, 4.6), so the abstract does not report a weaker baseline than the results and (b) is not observed. For context: the SIMP baseline (88-line MATLAB, same CPU) is by far the faster method in Table 1.

R3.evidence: Secs. 3.1-3.2: the PINN is trained from scratch inside each TO iteration without labelled data; its cost is part of the Table 1 times (R1/R2). Also quality stratum.

R4.evidence: Secs. 3.1.2, 4.1 and 4.3: PINNTO's compliance appears to come from the PINN displacement field [inferred]; no FE re-analysis of the returned PINNTO designs is described, and Sec. 4.3 explains PINNTO's lower coarse-mesh compliance by FEA inaccuracy, which suggests the two objectives come from different solvers. Achieved volume fractions and failure counts are not reported; Fig. 12 shows non-optimized results for small networks (qualitative only).

reporting.n_test_cases: 4 validation cases with times (Table 1); mesh study at 5 sizes and a 3D cantilever compared with SIMP without times; NN-size, passive-element and two-load cases without a SIMP comparison (Secs. 4.1-4.6)

notes: Screening code was I-UNCLEAR. Full-text inclusion: the energy-based PINN replaces the FE solver inside SIMP (per-problem learning, §3.1). method_family set to 'other': the PINN parameterizes the displacement field, not the design, so neural_reparam does not fit well. Primary outcome: the first quantitative classical comparison (Sec. 4.1, Fig. 7) and the abstract's emphasis are both design parity, so stratum Q; Table 1's speed result (PINNTO about 1,000 times slower) is recorded as an alternative and is a negative speed result reported by the authors (useful for C4). Reporting locators: CPU, library versions and per-iteration and total times = Sec. 3.2 and Table 1 (no warm-up or repeats; MATLAB vs PyTorch; hence timing_protocol_stated = partial); times only for the four validation cases (selective); no code or data statement. Inconsistencies for the verifier: convergence criterion 1% (Sec. 3.1.2) vs τ = 0.01% (Sec. 4.1); Table 1 vs Fig. 7 rounding; 3D gap 5.2% of the SIMP value vs the text's claim of under 5% (4.96% of the PINNTO value [derived]). Related records by the same group, judged separate studies, not duplicates: P00533 (CPINNTO, CMAME 2023), P00559 (Engineering Structures 2024), P00669 (FF-PINNTO, CMAME 2025) and P01420 (first author's thesis). Access: QUT ePrints institutional repository, generic User-Agent, no personal data. No author named Jun Wang. Adjudicator check (2026-09-24): the QUT ePrints accepted manuscript (landing page lists doi 10.1016/j.engstruct.2022.115484) was re-read in full; page numbers 'AAM p.' are the manuscript's own numbers, one less than the PDF page because of the repository cover page. The first quantitative classical comparison is the compliance comparison of Sec. 4.1 (Fig. 7 and the 'less than 2~3%' statement, AAM p. 17), which precedes the Table 1 times (AAM p. 20).

R2.reason: With stratum Q decided, R2 applies only through criterion (b) (§11), and (b) does not hold: the abstract (AAM p. 1) names SIMP without numbers, and the results compare with the same SIMP family (88-line code, Sec. 4.1, AAM p. 16; Liu and Tovar 3D code, Sec. 4.6). The second coder's pass assessed baseline efficiency under a speed stratum.

stratum.reason: The abstract (AAM p. 1) and conclusion (Sec. 5, AAM p. 27) claim only design parity with SIMP, without numbers or any speed claim. The main text's first quantitative classical comparison is the compliance gap of Sec. 4.1 (Fig. 7, 'less than 2~3%', AAM p. 17), before the Table 1 times (AAM p. 20), which the authors present as a limitation. §5.1 order and emphasis both give a quality-only primary outcome.

claimed_speedup.reason: Not a disputed item (the two values agree). With the primary outcome decided as quality only, the record follows the rule applied to every final non-speed record (adjudicated P00051 and P01813): the quality primary outcome carries no speed factor. The Table 1 ratios (AAM p. 20) stay in claimed_speedup_basis as the speed alternative.
